sentences.text: Dryosaurus is a genus of two known species of ornithopod dinosaurs that belong to the Dryosauridae family.
The genus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1894.
This dinosaur possessed a light and slender body form featuring a long neck, hind legs, and tail.
Its mouth included a horny beak and cheek teeth adapted for processing vegetation.
The animal had short arms with five fingers on each hand.
Specimens measured between 2.5 and 4.5 meters in total length and stood about 1.5 meters tall at the shoulders.
The name Dryosaurus comes from Greek words meaning 'tree' and 'lizard', reflecting a presumed forest-dwelling lifestyle rather than the shape of its teeth.
A hatchling found in Utah showed that young Dryosaurus had proportionally large eyes and short muzzles, which changed as they grew.
Researchers suggest that Dryosaurus cheeks may have been used to store food.
Samuel Wendell Williston discovered remains of small euornithopods in Albany County, Wyoming, in 1876.
The holotype specimen of Dryosaurus, cataloged as YPM 1876, was discovered in Reed YPM Quarry 5 within the Upper Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation.
Rodney D. Scheetz and his family discovered a Dryosaurus fossil site near Uravan, Colorado, in 1972.
Fossils have been found at sites including Bone Cabin Quarry, the Red Fork of the Powder River, and Lily Park.
Dryosaurus altus was originally named by Marsh in 1978 and remained the only valid species until Carpenter and Galton described Dryosaurus elderae in 2018.
Dryosaurus primarily ate low-growing vegetation found in ancient floodplain environments.
The animal subsisted mainly on low vegetation in ancient floodplains.
Dryosaurus was a quick and agile runner that used its stiff tail as a counterbalance while moving.
The always erect tail of Dryosaurus helped maintain balance while running.
Researchers suggest that Dryosaurus relied on its speed as its primary defense against carnivorous dinosaurs.
Skeletal characteristics indicate Dryosaurus was quite fast, relying on speed as its primary defense against carnivorous theropods.
Museum curator John Foster noted that Dryosaurus teeth were characterized by a strong median crest on the lateral surface.
A Dryosaurus juvenile found in Utah's Dinosaur National Monument confirmed that the species followed craniofacial development patterns similar to other vertebrates.
Dryosaurus shares size, shape, and bone characteristics with Hypsilophodontidae ornithopods but cannot be included in that family due to special genus characteristics.
Therefore, Dryosaurus has been assigned to its own family, Dryosauridae.
A cladogram of Dryosaurus follows the analysis by Paul M. Barrett, Richard J. Butler, Richard J. Twitchett, and Stephen Hutt in 2011.

The Morrison Formation, where Dryosaurus fossils are found, dates from 156.3 to 146.8 million years ago, corresponding to the late Oxfordian, Kimmeridgian, and early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic.
Dryosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages, approximately 154.8 to 143.1 million years ago.
Dryosaurus fossils have been found in what is now North America.
Fossil sites indicate that Dryosaurus was typically a forest-dwelling animal.
Dryosaurus shared its environment with giant sauropods including Brontosaurus, Camarasaurus, and Apatosaurus.
Dryosaurus lived alongside ornithischian herbivores such as Camptosaurus, Stegosaurus, and Othnielosaurus.
It is debated or unknown what the true adult size of Dryosaurus was because no adult specimens have been found.
Recent research by Krumenacker et al. (2026) describes three iguanodontian specimens from the Morrison Formation that have a morphology distinct from Dryosaurus and Camptosaurus.
